subsection: 3. Case study: the Coleraine University controversy

notes.h: Background: Northern Ireland, Derry and higher education
notes.b: To see why the choice of a university site caused a row, you first need to know how Northern Ireland was governed and what Derry's position in it was. Derry had a college but not a university, and its nationalist majority saw the choice of site as a test of fair treatment.
points: Northern Ireland was governed by a Unionist (mainly Protestant) government at Stormont, the seat of its parliament. Catholics and nationalists (who wanted a united Ireland) were a large minority, and Derry (Londonderry) had a Catholic nationalist majority.

Derry's local council, Londonderry Corporation, was controlled by unionists despite that majority, because ward boundaries were redrawn in 1936 in their favour. This meant the city's own representatives could not influence decisions about it.

Derry, the second largest city in Northern Ireland, suffered high unemployment and more emigration than the Belfast area. Its traditional industry of shirt-making employed mainly women, so male unemployment was especially high.

Magee College in Derry was founded in 1865 by the Presbyterian Church and taught degrees of Trinity College Dublin, so it was a college rather than a university. Before 1968 the only university in Northern Ireland was Queen's University Belfast.

The Robbins Report of 1963 recommended a large expansion of higher education across the United Kingdom. Robbins and the Lockwood Committee (appointed the same year) belong to the same wave of expansion, which made a second Northern Ireland university a live question.

Terence O'Neill became Prime Minister in 1963. His government's modernisation programme included expanding higher education, building new towns and economic planning, so the new university was part of a wider plan.

Derry nationalists argued that their city, with its existing college and decades of neglect, deserved the university, and many Derry unionists agreed. The site was therefore a test of whether Stormont treated the west of the province fairly.
Only one new university was planned, so choosing one town meant that no other town could host it. This is why the contest between towns was bound to leave a loser.
notes.tip: Examiners expect you to place any document or event in context: Lockwood, 1965, Derry. Be ready to say why Derry expected the university (second city, existing college, high unemployment, long neglect).

notes.h: The Lockwood Committee and the University for Derry campaign, 1963-1965
notes.b: The Lockwood Committee was set up to advise on the site, and in response a campaign in Derry, backed across the community, pressed for the city to be chosen.
points: The Lockwood Committee, chaired by Sir John Lockwood, was appointed in 1963 to advise on higher education in Northern Ireland, including the second university and where to place it.
The committee took evidence from the Derry campaign and from other towns, such as Coleraine, that were competing for the university.
The University for Derry Committee was formed to campaign for the city. John Hume, then a young teacher, was its chair, and it ran in 1964-65.

The campaign drew support from across the community: nationalists, some unionists and business people in Derry. This cross-community base made it harder for the government to dismiss it as purely nationalist.
The campaign argued that Derry had the population, the existing Magee College buildings and the need for jobs, and that the west deserved fair treatment.
Campaigners used meetings, pamphlets and slogans to put the case that Derry had been overlooked. This is propaganda in the sense of material used to shape opinion, not necessarily to deceive.
notes.tip: For a comparison of two documents on cross-community opposition, remember that nationalists and some unionists and business people backed the campaign. Say who supported it, not just that it existed.

notes.h: The Lockwood report and the Stormont decision, February 1965
notes.b: The Lockwood report chose Coleraine over Derry, Derry protested, and the government accepted the choice. Each step fed the belief in Derry that the decision was unfair.
points: The Lockwood report of February 1965 recommended Coleraine, in County Londonderry, rather than Derry. Coleraine is about 30 miles from Derry and much smaller. Do not confuse County Londonderry with the city.
Derry supporters answered with a motorcade (a convoy of vehicles) to Stormont in February 1965 to protest against the report.
Derry supporters alleged that 'faceless men', unseen people rather than an open process, had really decided the matter. No proof was offered, so this was an allegation and not an established fact.
The government accepted the report and won the Stormont debate and vote by its majority. Nationalist members and some Derry unionists opposed the decision.
The government's case for Coleraine was that it offered a central site, good access and room for expansion, as a planned new university town. It said Derry's case had been fully considered.
The campaign continued after the vote, and the grievance lasted for years. In Derry the decision was widely seen as a sign that Stormont would not give the city equal treatment in public investment.
notes.tip: For the Ordinary Level case for Coleraine, give the standard government reasons: central site, access, room for expansion. Always present 'faceless men' as an allegation by Derry supporters.

notes.h: Key personality: John Hume (part 1, the University for Derry campaign)
notes.b: Hume was the chair of the University for Derry campaign. The campaign made him a public figure, was an early step in his career and shaped the constitutional, cross-community approach that marked his later politics.
points: Who he was: John Hume was born in Derry in 1937, was educated in Derry and at St Patrick's College, Maynooth, and worked as a teacher. About 1960 he helped found a credit union (a community savings and loan society) in Derry.

What he did: he chaired the University for Derry Committee in 1964-65, organised across the community, and led public meetings and the protest. He was a leader of the campaign, a participant and not an observer.
Shaped by events: the defeat taught him that protest needed organisation and cross-community support, and the campaign made him a public figure in Derry.
Contemporaries: supporters saw him as a moderate and effective campaigner who could organise across the community. Some unionists saw him as a nationalist agitator.
Historians: they see the campaign as the start of his career and of his constitutional, cross-community approach to politics.
Pointer only: his later roles include the Derry Citizens' Action Committee in 1968, Stormont MP for Foyle in 1969, founder of the SDLP in 1970 and MP for Foyle from 1983.
notes.tip: On Hume as a part-1 personality, cover his role as chair, his cross-community base and what the campaign meant for his career. Do not narrate his later SDLP career.

notes.b: Putting the dates in order matters because essays on this controversy are rewarded for facts in sequence. The result was that Coleraine got the university and Derry did not.
points: 1963: the Robbins Report, the Benson Report and the Matthew Report all appear (three separate reports), and the Lockwood Committee is appointed.
1963 to 1965: the Lockwood Committee investigates sites and takes evidence, while the University for Derry Committee campaigns for Derry.
February 1965: the Lockwood report recommends Coleraine, and Derry supporters travel to Stormont by motorcade to protest.
1965: the Stormont government accepts the report and wins the vote by its majority.
1965 to 1968: planning and building of the new university at Coleraine proceed while the Derry campaign continues.
1968: the New University of Ulster opens at Coleraine, so Derry is left without a new university.
Magee College remained in Derry. In 1984 the New University of Ulster merged with Ulster Polytechnic to form the University of Ulster, and Magee later became a campus of that university.
notes.tip: Use the order Lockwood 1963, report February 1965, motorcade, Stormont vote, 1968 opening. Essays that only list the decision score poorly, so link each step to Derry's reaction.

notes.h: Propaganda, discrimination and the 'west of the Bann' grievance
notes.b: Both sides used the controversy to argue about fairness, and the decision became a symbol of regional and religious inequality. Two key concepts apply here: discrimination and propaganda.
points: Discrimination means unequal treatment because of religion or background. Here it is the claim that the location decision favoured the unionist east over the nationalist west.
Derry campaigners used posters, pamphlets, public meetings and the motorcade to present their case, and their message was that Derry had been overlooked.
The government and its supporters presented Coleraine as a sound academic and economic choice, and rejected charges of sectarian motives. This too was propaganda: material shaping opinion.

The 'west of the Bann' grievance (the River Bann runs through the north of the province) held that new industry, investment and public bodies were placed east of it, leaving Derry and the west with fewer jobs.
Critics linked the decision to other public investment decisions, such as Craigavon, designated in 1965, so it seemed one of a pattern rather than a single choice.

The controversy therefore fed a wider belief that discrimination was built into government decisions, not only into local councils. Nationalists argued they had no fair share of public investment, a view the civil rights movement later made central.
notes.tip: Define discrimination and propaganda as used in this case, and say that both sides used propaganda, not just the Derry campaign.

notes.h: Other west of the Bann grievances in the mid-1960s
notes.b: The university decision was one of several decisions of the mid-1960s that Derry nationalists saw as favouring the east, so examiners expect you to name at least two others.
points: The Benson Report of 1963 (by Sir Henry Benson) recommended closing unprofitable railway lines. The Derry Road line from Portadown through Omagh to Derry closed in 1965.
The closure ended the line through Omagh to Portadown and weakened the city's links with the south-west and the Dublin direction, which nationalists argued reinforced Derry's isolation.
The Matthew Report of 1963 (by Sir Robert Matthew) was a regional plan for growth around Belfast and proposed a new city between Lurgan and Portadown.

Craigavon, the new city between Lurgan and Portadown in County Armagh, was designated in 1965. It was seen in Derry as drawing investment east. It is named after Lord Craigavon, the first Prime Minister.
Derry's economic decline, with high unemployment, emigration and few new industries, made each decision against the west feel worse.
Unionist control of Londonderry Corporation meant Derry's own representatives could not influence these decisions.
Housing in Derry was overcrowded, which added to the sense that the city's needs were ignored.
notes.tip: Name at least two other grievances beyond the university, such as the rail closure, Craigavon, housing or local government.

notes.h: Significance for Derry, Hume and the civil rights movement
notes.b: The controversy mattered beyond one university because it gave Derry a concrete example of unfair treatment and gave Hume his first campaign.
points: For Derry, the decision confirmed a sense of neglect and gave nationalists a clear example of the discrimination grievance, which fed the civil rights movement in Derry.
For Hume, chairing a broad campaign gave him experience of organising across the community and a public reputation.
For the civil rights movement, the controversy showed that public investment could be a political issue, and it added to housing and voting grievances.
Unionists regarded the decision as a rational choice of site and an example of the government's modernising programme.
Historians view the decision as one of several episodes that deepened nationalist distrust of Stormont in the mid-1960s.
notes.tip: In essays on how Coleraine contributed to tension in Derry or to civil rights, state a clear thesis and link the decision to the wider west of the Bann pattern.

notes.h: Assessment: the Coleraine decision and discrimination
notes.b: Judging this controversy means weighing both sides' cases, strengths against limits, and contemporary views against later ones.
points: Strength of the nationalist case: Derry was larger, had Magee College's existing buildings and had high unemployment, which gave a strong economic argument.
Strength of the government's case: Coleraine offered a central site and room to grow, and a formal committee, the Lockwood Committee, had made the recommendation.
Limit of the nationalist case: the 'faceless men' allegation came with no proof of a plot, so it could not show that the decision was made on sectarian grounds.
Limit of the government's case: Coleraine was a small town, and the wider pattern of investment in the east weakened the claim that spending was spread evenly.
Contemporary view: Derry nationalists saw discrimination, while unionists saw a planning decision.
Later view: historians tend to see the controversy as a symbol of wider inequality rather than proof of a single plot.
Both sides agreed that Derry deserved higher education, so the dispute was about the site and not the principle.
notes.tip: Paired judgement points are rewarded: give the strength and limit of each side's case, contemporary against later views, and conclude that it was a symbol of inequality rather than proof of a plot.

keyTerms.definition: Unequal treatment of people because of their religion or background; nationalists saw the siting of the new university away from Derry as an example.
Materials and messages used to shape public opinion, which both the University for Derry campaign and the government used to argue their case.
The committee appointed in 1963 to examine possible sites for a new university in Northern Ireland and to recommend one.
The cross-community campaign of 1964 to 1965 that pressed for the new university to be sited in Derry, chaired by John Hume.
The university opened at Coleraine in 1968 as a result of the Lockwood recommendation.
The nationalist grievance that public investment and new industry were concentrated east of the River Bann, leaving the west and Derry with fewer jobs.
The Presbyterian college in Derry, founded in 1865, whose lack of university status was central to the case for a university in the city.
The 1963 report that recommended expanding higher education across the United Kingdom and prompted Northern Ireland's plan for a second university.
The 1963 transport report that recommended railway closures, including the Derry Road line, closed in 1965.
